Its extensive control of the financial system allows it to turn on a flood of bank loans when the economy looks weak, and restrain credit when the danger has passed. China’s avoidance of recession in at least the past three decades suggests that this form of credit-based stabilization is more effective than traditional, more indirect stimulation of the economy through government deficits and central bank monetary easing…When a recession threatens, the government tells banks to lend --— to local governments, construction companies and real estate developers. Then, if the credits go bad, the government swoops in and takes the nonperforming loans off of financial companies’ books. Uninterrupted rapid growth then shrinks the government debt as a percentage of gross domestic product, and the system sails blithely forward[.]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And here’s what I wrote in 2018:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>China…directed banks to lend lots more money [in 2009]. The World Bank </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f4e6f344-6add-40a3-a836-698c57dcbca8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">estimated</a><span> that increased bank credit represented 40 percent of China’s stimulus. Much of the lending </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/76e5382e-3e7b-4baf-ad22-c502830c13f7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">was done</a><span> by China’s four large state-owned banks. The money went to infrastructure, real estate and all kinds of corporate projects, many of which were carried out by the country’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ef1251de-b80e-475c-acec-da83b7ee9f13?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">state-owned</a><span> enterprises.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Basically, most countries use two types of policy to get the economy moving again when some sort of negative shock hits it: </p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">monetary policy (e.g. cutting interest rates), and</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">fiscal policy (e.g. stimulus spending).</p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Macroeconomists disagree about why interest rate cuts give the economy a boost, but most agree that the policy usually has an effect. Although there are many other theories and interpretations, one way you can think of rate cuts is as a </span><em>financial </em><span>policy — by making it easier for businesses to borrow and invest, low interest rates stimulate business activity. Fiscal policy, in contrast, pretty much bypasses the world of finance and aims directly at the real economy — you build a bridge or a road, which employs some people who might otherwise be unemployed, and then those people turn around and spend their money elsewhere in the economy, igniting a virtuous cycle of spending and working. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>China uses both of those, but it also uses a third policy: </span><em>financial</em><span> policy. Instead of simply cutting interest rates and hoping that this filters through to bank lending, China’s government uses its direct control over the banking system to push banks to lend more. In the 2010s, after the Great Recession and the 2015 Chinese stock crash, this mostly meant lending to real estate companies. This lending fueled the biggest property boom the world has ever seen. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The boom </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4d4a7568-6d0e-4ed7-b977-42ab8621f0a7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">ended in late 2021</a><span>. The crash of the Chinese property developer Evergrande began a sequence of bankruptcies and defaults across the entire real estate sector. One of them is that he is our first pump and dump president. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Hi, Paul Krugman here. That’s common knowledge. One of the things that is really amazing about it, however, is the way in which he enriched himself — a lot of which has to do with crypto.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So the New York Times had a report just the other day on Trumpcoin, the memecoin issued on Trump’s behalf which got a lot of buyers, a lot of money came flowing into it. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It should have been obvious from the beginning that the coin was inherently worthless, and at this point it essentially is worthless. It has lost 97 percent of its value. But a lot of people did buy in at the high prices.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What was special about the New York Times story was two things. First, they put a number on how much money naive investors have lost on the coin, which is 3.8 billion dollars. And even more surprising is the number of people who were in effect suckers here — almost a million.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s really amazing. I mean, I was completely cynical but I didn’t think there were that many suckers out there. But it turns out there were really a lot. A few people made money off the coin — basically insiders who got to buy it early and then were able to cash in before the broader retail market realized that this was a worthless token. There’s another token, the World Liberty Financial coin — which has also crashed, although the Times had difficulty in tracking down how many people have lost how much money. There’s the Melania coin. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Okay, all of this is amazing. As Trump would say, it’s like nothing anybody’s ever seen before. I think we should say, however, that this is a bigger story than just the Trump coin, and it’s a bigger story than just Trump himself.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What we’re witnessing is or has been a really enormous pump and dump scheme, I would argue, involving more or less all of crypto. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So if you don’t know the background, Trump used to be highly critical of cryptocurrency, saying it was worthless and a scam, which was true. But then when it became clear that there was money in it for him, he reversed course. And during the 2024 election, crypto interests contributed a lot of money to Trump. They then after the election poured a lot of money into his own enrichment, into his own projects. And the administration came in with a very pro crypto stance: deregulation encouraging uses of crypto, at least talk about a national bitcoin reserve, all of that. And the price of bitcoin doubled after the election; the valuation, the market cap of cryptocurrency in general went from a little over two trillion to more than four trillion.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And then starting last fall it all came crashing down. Not all the way to zero — the price of Bitcoin right now as I record this is about what it was on the eve of the 2024 election; it’s about half what it was at its peak. That’s also true, roughly speaking for the market cap. So we’ve seen about two trillion dollars of market valuation wiped out.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why is this a pump and dump story? Well what is cryptocurrency good for? As you know, I’ve been on this for a long time. Bitcoin was introduced in 2009 — this is a seventeen year old idea which has yet to find any legitimate use cases. Illegitimate use cases, yes. There was also a report in the Wall Street Journal about the extent to which Iran and North Korea have been making use of cryptocurrency to evade U.S. sanctions, so there is that. But it’s still not enough to justify a multi-trillion dollar asset.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Anyway, it was trendy, it was exciting, it was fashionable and particularly after November 2024 it was pushed with the encouragement of the Trump Administration. It was just a heavy marketing campaign that had the advantage of also having the authority or whatever, the credibility — such as it was but among some people real —of Donald Trump behind it. They all evaporated.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think we can say that to some extent what happened was that Trump kind of moved on to other things. There also is some distracted boyfriend meme: the guy looking over his shoulder. A lot of the excitable, fear of missing out, latest thing money has probably moved from crypto to AI. So that might have happened even without Trump. But the basic story is that Trump guided, pushed people into a whole asset class, crypto, of which a large part is Bitcoin, but other stuff as well. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We don’t know how much, or I don’t know, how much crypto was bought during this period, but it has to be substantial. And then it crashed. And at this point, essentially anybody who bought crypto during this era, since the 2024 election, has lost money.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s a  lot of money; we know that on paper — it’s not really paper, but anyway — in principle two trillion dollars has been lost in crypto. Now a lot of that is probably money just given back, imaginary gains that took place during the run-up. But a substantial amount of additional money was from people who did buy in during this whole episode. So this has to be many times the size of the losses on the Trump coin.  And it is, I would say, at a functional level another pump and dump scheme.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this case the beneficiaries were people who were already in crypto. Clearly some of the crypto interests that bought themselves a president probably stayed fully invested. But others must have cashed out, and a lot of innocents — well a lot of a lot of suckers, let’s not mince words here — a lot of suckers clearly lost a lot of money.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s an extraordinary thing. There have been pump and dump schemes forever, probably going back to the Phoenicians or something. But this is on a scale we’ve never seen, and with the president of the United States in the center of it. Which I guess given everything else comes as no surprise.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Happy 250th birthday, America.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. One of the things they say is “we are capitalist, not socialist,” which is definitely a sentiment that I agree with.  </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Suozzi said on the panel, very correctly, that market economies have dramatically outperformed the competition and delivered, while not perfect societies, certainly the greatest levels of material prosperity that we see anywhere on Earth. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is all totally correct, but I think that people who know that it’s correct need to think more about why, despite its correctness, it has become so unfashionable for young people to embrace capitalism. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I think one really important reason is that if you look at what people spend money on, you know housing and health care are the two most important sectors by far. Young people consume far below-average amounts of health care, though, meaning that their consumption is really dominated by housing. A large share of the population consumes housing in the form of renting a home from themselves, so they are somewhat insulated from the ups and downs of the housing market. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But those people are mostly old. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you’re young, your experience of the economy is dominated by the housing situation. And the housing situation in the United States is not very good. So I think for most young people “capitalism” means something like “the status quo system,” and they perceive the status quo system to be pretty bad because they are super exposed to the single most dysfunctional element of the status quo economic system. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, in my capacity as a lawyer for capitalism, I am happy to point out that not only is housing the most dysfunctional element of the status quo economy, </span><em>but</em><span> </span><em>it’s also the element that is run in the least capitalistic way</em><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Far and away the number one thing that could improve young people’s living standards in America would be to embrace more market-oriented housing policies. But for anyone to understand that, those inclined to tout the virtues of capitalism need to embrace that idea. As a political pragmatist, I don’t really blame Suozzi for blasting efforts to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6a6218d3-864d-4332-a0d7-67ab02cd67af?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">foist zoning reform on his constituents on Long Island</a><span> a few years ago since his district is a wretched hive of NIMBYism. But younger people’s lived experience of “capitalism” is of central planning and massive shortages of the single most important item they consume. So of course if people tell them the alternative to the status quo is “socialism,” a lot of them are going to want that. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">America’s slow-motion housing crisis </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, on one level, housing in the United States </span><em>is</em><span> very capitalistic. The overwhelming majority of it is constructed with private capital and sold or rented for profit. Most homes are also privately owned — mostly by owner-occupants but with a significant sector of small-time landlords and a handful of large-scale ones, too. Public and nonprofit housing do exist in the United States, but they are a relatively small niche. The result is a housing sector awash in private capital and profit-seeking. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What it lacks is much in the way of free markets. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And these anti-market policies have grown up, over time, in insidious ways and merged to create a situation where, by 2026, we are dealing with systemic housing shortages almost everywhere in the country. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This mess all goes back 100 years to the Supreme Court’s Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty decision, which determined that it is perfectly legitimate to make apartment buildings illegal on certain swaths of land. This is just a huge contravention of the basic logic of free enterprise. It’s not that everyone — or even most people, or even a particularly large minority of people — ought to live in multi-family dwellings. But a small apartment on cheap land is an obvious method of housing low-income people, and low-income people need places to live. And where land is </span><em>expensive</em><span>, stacking dwellings vertically is the most normal and obvious way to ensure that supply and demand curves can balance out. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But widespread midcentury apartment bans did not produce an acute crisis, because of the widespread adoption of the automobile. The fact that it was newly feasible to build much more suburban housing was a huge positive shock to supply in the postwar generation, and that development more than outweighed the impact of bad policy. By the late 1960s, much of this new suburban housing was manufactured homes built in factories. In the 1970s, however, new rules went into effect that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bd4b7433-b1f2-40c2-b251-c71ca70b4fd1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">greatly restricted manufactured housing</a><span>. The late 1970s and the 1980s then saw the rise of the “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/154c0082-c6cc-4062-a732-634413b1454a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">growth control</a><span>” movement in the Northeast and California, which sought to halt suburban sprawl in the name of preserving open space. So by the 1990s, you couldn’t build apartments or manufactured homes on most land, and you couldn’t build suburban sprawl around San Francisco or Los Angeles or New York or Boston. But in </span><em>most</em><span> of America, a metro area could grow outward and housing remained relatively affordable. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Then, after 2008, a consensus developed that too many people were getting mortgages, so we made it harder to finance new suburban starter homes on top of everything else. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For a little while the impact of this wasn’t so notable, but for the past decade or so — since the labor market normalized — we’ve been living in a kind of Everywhere Shortage. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My account of the phases of this crisis follows the work of Kevin Erdmann, who </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6a7694a7-07bb-41b1-bd0d-b6c9b3840c8a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">calculates that we’re about 15 million total units short</a><span>. Erdmann was also the first to observe the importance of incorporating events such as the 1970s crackdown on manufactured homes into our understanding of the lead-up to the Great Recession.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But the upshot is that we’re in a really bad situation in this country.</p><p optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Ideas versus vibes</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Notably, the people who constructed America’s system of widespread comprehensive central planning of the housing market did not typically think of themselves as socialists. And certainly, the typical suburban homeowner regards it as his God-given right to block new development and change in his neighborhood. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you’re an older, reasonably prosperous homeowner, this bad situation probably doesn’t have a negative impact on you. And you almost certainly don’t think of yourself as a communist who strongly favors central planning and believes free markets are nonsense. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you’re a young person facing higher rents and despairing about getting on the path to homeownership, you probably don’t think of yourself as a victim of a failed socialist economic experiment the way a refugee fleeing Cuba or Venezuela would. The victims of bad housing policy hear people talking about how America is a great free-market success story, so if they feel that the success story is not working for them personally, they conclude that capitalism and free markets are in fact a big failure.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I would also note that the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act passed with overwhelming bipartisan support, but </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/71c0c186-5ab9-445e-94c0-f0f9ed6bd497?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">all of the “no” votes came from Republicans</a><span>. And what those Republicans were objecting to was not the NEPA waivers, manufactured-home deregulation, or regulatory favors for community banks — it was some fairly small incentives to try to get localities to change their zoning. One of the main reasons that statewide zoning reforms keep failing in the Northeast is that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/358b95ea-c12f-42ec-bb07-7fe8f5bc4803?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Acela Corridor Republicans oppose them</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In Maine and New Hampshire and California, Republicans have seen YIMBYism as a form of deregulation and backed it, so big bills have passed. But in New York and Maryland and New Jersey and Connecticut, they’ve seen it as trampling on the sanctity of local control, and it’s been very hard to get anything done. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These are the most invisible people in the discourse relative to their practical significance in American politics. Not just because they directly block housing (though they do block housing), but because politically cautious moderate Democrats fear a backlash </span><em>from the right</em><span> if they embrace housing deregulation. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Obviously, I do not agree with right-NIMBYs on the merits. But they are important, and I think there is remarkably little engagement with their views. What you tend to get is either name-calling leftists asserting these types are racist, or else Manhattan Institute types rationalizing away the bad behavior of northeastern Republicans. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It seems to me, though, that if you want to understand youth socialism, you need to understand why middle-aged and elderly conservatives see opposition to new housing as consistent with their support for capitalism. In their view when you buy a home in a single-family neighborhood, part of what you are buying is the single-familyness of the entire neighborhood. Left-NIMBYs see zoning reform as free-market deregulation, so they are against it. But right-NIMBYs see zoning reform as contravening their property rights, so they are against it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The truth is, this kind of dispute speaks to issues that long predate the whole idea of socialism. It’s an older one about what property rights even are.</p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The war for simple property rights</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you go back to the emergence of what we understand as capitalism, the prior system was, of course, not socialism but feudalism. And a key aspect of pre-capitalist property rights is that they tended to be very complicated. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In Jane Austen’s Regency-era novels, the characters are constantly grappling with parcels of land that are encumbered by complicated entailments. By our modern lights, the idea that Mr. Bennet could be prohibited from leaving his estate to his daughters is bizarre. It’s either his estate or it’s not. But the traditional mode of thinking was that if an estate is someone’s property, then he has the right to attach whatever kind of stipulation to his property that he wants. When the property is then inherited by someone new, that person inherits the stipulations. To say everyone can do whatever they want with the property that they own would be a major violation of property rights because property rights include the right to impose these irrevocable stipulations. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Thinking about it logically, if entailments can attach to a piece of property but can never be removed, then over the long term all property will be encumbered — and over time it will be encumbered by an increasing number of stipulations. Eventually, all commerce will be strangled by the whims of various long-dead previous owners. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What happened instead was that over the course of the 19th century, various acts of Parliament restricted entailments. And the whole process of creating capitalism was full of measures like this. Pre-modern property rights were very complicated. People had joint shares in communally owned fields. There were all kinds of complicated partial-use rights to various parcels of land that couldn’t be bought or sold. Simplifying these rights made it much easier to undertake various kinds of transactions and engage in modern commerce and growth. Because the British political system of the time was elite-dominated, this was often done on inequitable terms. But it unleashed a ton of growth and made the vast majority of people better off on average. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the modern world, we have recreated a system of complicated property rights. The conventional understanding is that owning a parcel of residential land gives you extensive authority to veto things that your neighbors might want to do, such as redevelop their parcel as townhouses or a small apartment building. In exchange for getting those rights vis-a-vis your neighbors, you lose the right to do what you want with your own land. The people who like the status quo mostly don’t conceive of it as a statist imposition on their personal property rights; they see it as property rights functioning naturally. And the young renters who are locked out of economic opportunity by the status quo </span><em>also</em><span> see this as property rights functioning naturally, and thus they become socialists. But the thing that would solve this problem is not a giant, economically wasteful program of public housing construction. It’s shifting to a regime of simplified property rights where everyone has much less authority over their neighbors’ land and much more authority over their own. </span></p><p class="button-wrapper" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">On the left, there’s a longstanding view that “abundance” and “YIMBYs” are just sock puppets for billionaires trying to bolster the legitimacy of capitalism. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">To this I say — if only! </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s genuinely true that it would do enormous good for the interests of America’s billionaires and C.E.O.s to see radical housing reform sweep the country. That’s in part because faster economic growth is good for everyone, including billionaires and C.E.O.s. But it’s mostly because, exactly as the leftists fear, housing abundance (and its natural complements like abundance of transportation and electricity transmission infrastructure) would bolster the legitimacy of capitalism. If “capitalism” meant “a system where demand for housing is met by rising quantities of housing rather than rising prices of housing,” then a lot more people would enjoy capitalism. But in a world where “capitalism” means “policy defers to the most risk-averse incumbent homeowners around,” a lot of people naturally feel that capitalism is not working for them. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But YIMBYism is dramatically worse-funded than the various NIMBY community groups that are propped up by mainstream foundations. Businesses lobby furiously on picayune regulations and tax policy matters, but the collective action problem in lobbying for housing reform is hard to overcome. And politically engaged venture capitalists and C.E.O.s are much more inclined to whine on Twitter about anti-capitalism than to cut large checks to the people trying to make capitalism actually work. I can’t think of any examples of someone pumping money into a primary that features a YIMBY Republican state legislator trying to give the boot to a NIMBY incumbent. For all the discussion of these issues over the past few years, there is still remarkably little money going into the relevant advocacy. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And this creates a dilemma for moderate Democrats. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Part of the point of moderation is to be politically savvy and politically cautious, and obviously calling for large-scale land-use reforms is risky. But another part of the point of moderation is to solve actual problems rather than being trapped by ideological dogmas. It just happens to both be true that capitalism + a welfare state is a much better system than socialism, and also that the economic status quo is not working well for young people. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The good news for markets is that the specific thing that’s not working well is housing — and housing is a problem where the solution is more markets. But this is only going to be persuasive if people are willing to say it and really push to do something about it. There is risk in pushing for big change, but there are also clearly a lot of people who are sick of the status quo and eager to see big change. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Should that change be socialism? Or should it be solving the problem at hand? I know what I think. </p><p class="button-wrapper"
